Anatomy of the Respiratory System
• The respiratory system is divided into 2 zones:
• Conducting zone
• All passageways for air
• Allow low resistance to air flow
• Filter, warm, and humidify air before entering alveoli
• Voice production
• Respiratory zone
• Respiratory bronchioles (smallest bronchiole) and alveoli
• Actual site of gas exchange

Anatomy of the Respiratory System

text:
Anatomy of the Respiratory System
• Respiratory zone structure
• The alveolar walls are composed of 1 layer of squamous epithelial cells, called “type I cells”.
• The external surface of type I cells is covered by a thin basement membrane.
• A dense network of thin-wall capillaries surrounds the alveolus.
• Together, the alveolar wall, basement membrane, and the capillary wall form the respiratory membrane.
• Gas exchange occurs by simple diffusion across the respiratory membrane.

Mechanics of Breathing
• Pulmonary ventilation - “Breathing”
• consists of two phases
• Inspiration: gases flow into lungs
• Expiration: gases exit lungs
• Important basic sequence:
• (1) Muscle movements
• (2) Volume changes
• (3) Pressure changes
• (4) Flows of air

Mechanics of ventilation
● Inspiratory muscles

text:
Inspiration
Inspiratory muscles contract
(diaphragm descends; rib cage rises).
Thoracic cavity volume increases.
Lungs are stretched.
Intrapulmonary volume increases.
Intrapulmonary pressure
drops to -1 mmHg.
Air flows into lungs down the pressure
gradient until intrapulmonary pressure is 0.

Inspiration

text:
Expiration
Inspiratory muscles relax
(diaphragm rises; rib cage descends due to recoil of
costal cartilages).
Thoracic cavity volume decreases.
Elastic lungs recoil passively.
Intrapulmonary volume decreases.
Intrapulmonary pressure
rises to +1 mmHg.
Air flows out of lungs down the pressure gradient
until intrapulmonary pressure is 0.

• Several respiratory volumes can be used to assess status of pulmonary ventilation
• Respiratory volumes can be combined to calculate respiratory capacities, which can give information on a person’s respiratory status
• Respiratory volumes and capacities are usually abnormal in people with pulmonary disorders
• Spirometer: original clinical tool used to measure patient’s respiratory volumes

text:
Mechanics of Breathing
• Anatomical dead space
• Volume of air that does not take part in gas exchange
• Consists of air that remains in conducting zone
• Average 150 ml out of 500 ml TV
• Alveolar dead space
• Should be zero in healthy person
• Space occupied by nonfunctional alveoli
• Can be due to collapse or obstruction
• Total dead space
• sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space

• Pulmonary Function Test
• Spirometry can distinguish
• Obstructive pulmonary disease: increased airway resistance (example: bronchitis)
• TLC, FRC, RV may increase TLC
• Restrictive disease: reduced TLC due to disease (example: tuberculosis) or exposure to environmental agents (example: fibrosis) TLC
• VC, TLC, FRC, RV decrease because lung expansion is compromised

text:
Mechanics of Breathing
• Pulmonary Function Test ○ Forced vital capacity (FVC) ■ amount of gas forcibly expelled after taking deep breath ○ Forced expiratory volume (FEV) ■ amount of gas expelled during specific time interval of FVC FVC ■ FEV 1: amount of air expelled in 1st second ○ Healthy individuals can expel 80% of FVC in 1st second
○ Patients with obstructive disease exhale less than 80% in 1st second
○ Patients with restrictive disease exhale 80% or more even with reduced FVC

text:
Mechanics of Breathing
• Minute Ventilation (MV)
• total amount of gas that flows into or out of respiratory tract in 1 minute
• Normal at rest: Average 6 L/min
• Normal with exercise: Up to 200 L/min
• Only rough estimate of respiratory efficiency
• MV = TV × Respiratory Rate
• Example: TV = 500 ml; Respiratory Rate = 14 breaths/min
MV = 500 × 14 = 7000 ml/min

text:
Mechanics of Breathing
• Alveolar ventilation (AV)
• Flow of gases into and out of respiratory zone in 1 minute
• Volume of dead space is taken into account in AV
• Better indicator of effective ventilation
• AV = (TV - Dead space) × Respiratory Rate
• Example: TV = 500 ml; Respiratory Rate = 14 breaths/min; Dead space = 150 ml
AV = (500 – 150) × 14 = 4900 ml/min

text:
Gas Exchange between Lungs and Blood
• Partial pressures and gas concentrations
• (1) The pressure exerted by each gas (Partial Pressure) in a mixture of gases is directly proportional to the percentage of the gas in the mixture.
• E.g. 21% O 2 & 760 mmHg
• P O2 = 160 mmHg
• (2) When a mixture of gases dissolves in liquid, the concentration of each gas in the liquid will be directly proportional to its partial pressure.
• i.e. higher partial pressure ⇒ higher concentration
• partial pressure gradient ⇒ concentration gradient
• When gas diffuse across the respiratory membrane
• Region of higher partial pressure → Region of lower partial pressure
• Down the partial pressure gradient!!!

text:
Transport of Gases in Blood
• Oxygen Transport
• Molecular O 2 is carried in blood in two ways:
• (1) 1.5% is dissolved in plasma 1.5%
• (2) 98.5% is loosely bound to each Fe atom of hemoglobin (Hb) in RBCs 98.5%
• Each Hb molecule is composed of four polypeptide chains, each with 1 iron- containing heme group
• So each Hb can transport four oxygen molecules
• Oxyhemoglobin (HbO 2 ): hemoglobin-O 2 combination
• Deoxyhemoglobin (HHb): hemoglobin that has released O 2

text:
Transport of Gases in Blood
• In lungs, the deoxyhemoglobin molecules (HHb) uptake O 2 and become oxyhemoglobin (HbO 2 )
• HHb + O 2 →HbO 2
• In tissues, the HbO 2 dissociates again and the O 2 diffuses into tissue cells for metabolic reactions
• HbO 2 →HHb + O 2

Transport of Gases in Blood
• Carbon Dioxide Transport
• CO 2 is transported in blood in three ways:
• (1) 10% is dissolved in plasma 10%
• (2) 20% is bound to the globin part of hemoglobin and become carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO 2 ) 20%
• Hb + CO 2 → HbCO 2
• (3) 70% is transported as bicarbonate ions in plasma 70%
• CO 2 combining with water in red blood cells to form carbonic acid, which quickly dissociates into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions in plasma

text:
Transport of Gases in Blood
• Influence of CO 2 on blood pH
• The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system is very important to keep normal blood pH.
• Normal range of blood pH: 7.35-7.45
• Change in respiratory rate can change blood pH by altering amount of carbonic acid in blood.
• Slow, shallow breathing→More CO 2 remain in blood →More carbonic acid→Blood pH decreases (Acidic)
• Rapid, deep breathing→Less CO 2 remain in blood →Less carbonic acid→Blood pH increases (Alkaline)

text:
Control of Breathing
• Respiratory rhythms are regulated by voluntary and involuntary control mechanisms
• Voluntary control of breathing
• Human can exert conscious control over the rate and depth of our breathing.
• The cerebral motor cortex send signals to motor neurons that control the respiratory muscles.
• The respiratory centers in brainstem are bypassed.
• However, the ability of holding breathe voluntarily is limited.

Control of Breathing
• Involuntary control of breathing
• When these peripheral chemoreceptors detect decreased levels of P O 2, increased levels of P CO 2, or decreased blood pH
• They fire more neural signals to respiratory centers in brainstem
• via sensory nerve fibers in vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) and glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX)
